name: Relative
tagline: A personal relationship tracker: who you know, when you last talked, who you are overdue to contact.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The data model here is embarrassingly simple: people, notes, interactions, a contact cadence, and a query for who is overdue. An agent will hand you a working local version in an afternoon and the schema will be correct on the first try. What it will not hand you is the part that makes these apps actually work, which is being on your phone at the moment you remember someone exists. Contact import, two-way sync, and push reminders are where the weekend goes, and a nudge that only exists in a browser tab on your laptop is a nudge you will stop reading by week three. Build it if you live in a browser anyway, otherwise expect real gaps.
coreLoopDIY: Stores people with notes and an interaction log, assigns each one a contact cadence, and shows you a daily list of who has gone cold.
requirements: A vCard export from your phone or Google Contacts for the initial import
Something to run a daily script if you want a digest: cron, launchd, or just opening the app
whatYouLose: A phone app, which is where relationship nudges either work or die
Contact sync, so your list drifts out of date the moment you meet someone new
Push notifications and a polished daily digest
Any calendar or email signal that auto-logs an interaction for you
Someone else worrying about your backups
moatNotes: The schema is trivial and the habit design is not. Most personal CRMs die from friction, so the only defensible work is making logging take two seconds on a phone.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the hard part of a personal CRM was never the database, it was remembering to open it. A paid app earns its money by living on the home screen, pulling contacts in automatically, and nagging you at a time you will actually read. A self-hosted version solves the storage problem perfectly and the behavior problem not at all, which is why so many people have a half-built relationship tracker rotting in a folder somewhere.
notes: The build is easy, the habit is not. Budget your effort accordingly.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal relationship tracker that runs on my machine. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js (App Router, TypeScript) with server actions
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/relative.db, created on first run
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- Everything runs with: npm install && npm run dev

Data model:
- person: id, name, how_we_met, location, notes (markdown text), cadence_days (nullable), archived (bool), created_at
- tag: id, label; person_tag join table
- interaction: id, person_id, happened_on (date), channel (call | text | email | in-person | other), note

Screens:
1. Dashboard: an "overdue" list of people where days since their most recent interaction exceeds cadence_days, sorted by most overdue first. Next to each, a one-click "log interaction" button that records today with channel "other" and lets me add a note inline.
2. People list: searchable by name, notes, and tag. Filter by tag. Show last contact date and cadence.
3. Person detail: editable fields, tag editor, full interaction history newest first, add-interaction form with a date picker.

Also build:
- A vCard (.vcf) import at /import that parses FN, EMAIL, TEL, NOTE and creates people, skipping exact name duplicates. Show a preview before committing.
- A JSON export endpoint that dumps the whole database, because this is my data.
- A script at scripts/digest.ts that prints today's overdue list to stdout so I can wire it to cron myself.

Explicitly out of scope: authentication, multi-user, mobile apps, push notifications, email sending, calendar or Gmail integration, any third-party API.

Seed the database with 8 fake people and a scattering of interactions so the dashboard is not empty on first run. Write a README with the two commands I need and nothing else. If any config is needed, read it from .env and commit a .env.example.
